newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Vietnam coffee comes out, quality concerns on hold.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam coffee comes out, quality concerns on hold.

text.p: Vietnam's robusta coffee crop is coming in at full spate on the back of dry weather in the main producing province of Dak Lak and total exports could reach 250,000 tonnes, regional traders said on Wednesday.
"The crop is coming in at full force. Exports could reach 230,000 to 240,000 tonnes. 250,000 tonnes, I would be surprised," the chief coffee dealer of a European commodity house said.
Traders said the Vietnamese have "exerted tremendous efforts" to nip any potential problems about mould hitting the beans.
"The beans are fine," one senior European dealer said. "We've received no call-backs so far" from coffee roasters.
Dealers said more than 50 percent of Vietnam's coffee beans had been committed to buyers.

The price of Vietnam's Grade 2 coffee was quoted by regional traders at around US$900-$940 a tonne FOB Saigon, up slightly from the previous week's level of around $850-$880 a tonne FOB from the same port.

"The rains have stopped and the crop is coming out strongly," said a trader in a Singapore-based trading firm which tracks the Vietnamese crop closely. The coffee season in Vietnam usually runs from November to late February.

Rains pounded Dak Lak late last year, hindering the drying of the beans and raising concerns over mould. Those worries now appear to be on hold, the traders said. Dak Lak produces about two-thirds of Vietnam's coffee exports.
"The coffee beans which were shipped out earlier will be arriving now with the roasters. A lot will really depend on the tolerance of the industry," a senior dealer said.

Most regional dealers also discounted the chances of an African-led initiative to cut exports further at a time when Indonesia's robusta crop is maturing and will start reaching the market in late-March.

A plan put forward by the Ivory Coast and Uganda called for an export reduction of 2.5 million 60-kg bags in the first six months of 1997 out of total exports of 53.5 million bags agreed by the ACPC last May.
The two African countries, along with Indonesia, were supposed to take the entire cut on themselves, dealers here said. The plan will be discussed in a special ACPC meeting on January 23 in Brazil.
"Why should Indonesia carry the baby on this and let someone else sneak in and grab their market share," one dealer said.

The country which would be ideally positioned to defy the African plan and sneak away with a part of Indonesia's market share is Vietnam, which is not expected to join the 14-member Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) any time soon. Weather conditions in Indonesia, Asia's largest producer of robusta coffee, remain ideal, traders said.
"I hear it's going to be a good crop and exports should reach 330,000-340,000 tonnes," one dealer said, adding exports last year were about 320,000 tonnes.
But another trader was more cautious.
"It's pure guesswork at the moment what the crop is going to be like," he said.
Prices of Indonesia's benchmark Grade 4 coffee were about $1,125-$1,150 a tonne FOB Panjang, dealers said. Business was at a minimum since most of the crop has long been sold.
LIFFE robusta coffee futures were seen opening later on Wednesday up to $80 higher on the back of New York's strong close and news about Brazil's bullish crop estimate, traders said.
"I think it's due $70 to $80 higher because of New York and the news of Brazil's crop estimate," one dealer said.
Trading of the robusta coffee contract in the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) was flat.
There were no trades done on Tuesday and total volume on Monday was a mere 120 tonnes.
About 60 tonnes of the May 1997 contract was traded at $1,072 a tonne while 60 tonnes of the July contract was traded at $1,067 a tonne.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
